paragraphs: Farmer John has N cows (1 ≤ N ≤ 20) of heights a₁…aₙ. His barn has N stalls with max height limits b₁…bₙ (so for example, if b₅ = 17, then a cow of height at most 17 can reside in stall 5).
In how many distinct ways can Farmer John arrange his cows so that each cow is in a different stall, and so that the height limit is satisfied for every stall?
inputFormat: The second line contains N space-separated integers a₁, a₂, …, aₙ.
The third line contains N space-separated integers b₁, b₂, …, bₙ. All heights and limits are in the range [1, 10⁹].
outputFormat: Print the number of ways Farmer John can place each cow into a different stall such that the height limit is satisfied for every stall. Note that the large size of the output might require the use of a 64-bit integer, like a "long long" in C++ or "long" in Java.

sampleExplanation.title: Sample Analysis
sampleExplanation.detail: Place the tallest cow (height 4) first: she fits in 2 stalls (limits 4 and 4). Next, cow of height 3 fits in 3 stalls total, minus the 1 stall already taken = 2 choices. Cow of height 2 fits in all 4 stalls minus 2 taken = 2 choices. Cow of height 1 gets the remaining 1 stall: 2 × 2 × 2 × 1 = 8.

hints.title: Why N! Brute Force Is Too Slow
hints.body: When N = 20, 20! ≈ 2.4 × 10¹⁸, so checking all permutations will Time Limit Exceed! Which cow has the strictest requirement?

hints.title: Place Cows from Tallest to Shortest!
hints.body: Sort the cows in descending order: a₀ ≥ a₁ ≥ … ≥ aₙ₋₁. Notice that ANY stall occupied by an earlier (taller) cow was ALSO tall enough for the current cow aᵢ!

hints.title: Multiply Available Choices
hints.body: For the i-th tallest cow (0-indexed), let fit(i) be the total number of stalls with bⱼ ≥ aᵢ. Since all i previously placed cows are ≥ aᵢ, all i of their stalls are among those fit(i) stalls! So cow i has exactly max(0, fit(i) − i) valid stalls left. Multiply these counts using a 64-bit integer!

editorial.summary: Sort cow heights in descending order. When placing the i-th tallest cow (0-indexed), every previously placed cow had height ≥ a[i] and therefore took one of the stalls with limit ≥ a[i]. If cnt is the number of stalls with b[j] ≥ a[i], there are (cnt − i) choices for cow i. Multiply over all i using 64-bit integers.
editorial.complexity: Time: O(N²) or O(N log N)  |  Space: O(N)

solutions.python:
import sys

def solve():
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
    n = data[0]
    a = sorted(data[1:1 + n], reverse=True)
    b = data[1 + n:1 + 2 * n]
    ans = 1
    for i, height in enumerate(a):
        fit = sum(1 for limit in b if limit >= height)
        choices = fit - i
        if choices <= 0:
            ans = 0
            break
        ans *= choices
    print(ans)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    solve()
